claims.text: The starting catalyst contains multiple principal elements, including platinum-group and base metals, in nearly equiatomic proportions.
The starting catalyst has no pronounced surface segregation.
The starting catalyst has no established nanoscale phase structures.
Thermal-redox cycling between 200 and 400 °C will induce a self-organized biphase surface layer.
The induced surface layer will contain nanoscale noble-metal clusters.
The induced surface layer will contain refractory oxide patches derived from the base metals.
Alternating reducing and oxidizing exposures drive selective surface segregation.
During reducing pulses, platinum-group metals become mobile.
During reducing pulses, platinum-group metals aggregate into nanoscale clusters.
During oxidizing pulses, some base metals convert into stable refractory oxide patches.
The refractory oxide patches physically anchor the noble-metal clusters.
Anchoring by refractory oxide patches inhibits sintering and aggregation of noble-metal clusters.
Inhibited sintering maintains a high catalytically active surface area during transient operation and thermal aging.
The redox-cycled catalyst will lose activity more slowly than the untreated catalyst under low-temperature transient exhaust conditions containing H2O and NO.
The redox-cycled catalyst will have greater durability than the untreated catalyst during thermal aging.
The proposed treatment will preserve low platinum-group-metal consumption.
The untreated catalyst typically undergoes accelerated degradation, activity loss, and sintering under transient exhaust exposure and thermal aging.
Overly aggressive thermal shocks or uncontrolled gas compositions may cause detrimental phase segregation or inactive-phase formation.
